sentences.text: Hi, I'm Tushar Patel, a software engineering student at Northeastern.
This is my final project for INFO 7375: Agent Proving Ground.

beats.narration_text: AI coding agents are good at saying they're finished. But "done" is a claim, not a result. An agent can fix the bug, or quietly edit the test so it passes, or just give up, and its message can look the same each time.

sentences.text: AI coding agents are good at saying they're finished.
But "done" is a claim, not a result.
An agent can fix the bug, or quietly edit the test so it passes, or just give up, and its message can look the same each time.

beats.narration_text: Agent Proving Ground is a command-line tool, with its code in a public GitHub repo. You give it a small coding task. It runs an AI agent on that task inside a locked sandbox, records every step it takes, and decides pass or fail by running its own tests. Never by taking the agent's word for it.

beats.narration_text: Parts of this already exist. E2B provides sandboxes for running AI-generated code. Langfuse records LLM traces and scores. Each solves one piece well. But a sandbox doesn't tell you whether the work is right, and a trace doesn't stop an agent from doing what it shouldn't.

E2B provides sandboxes for running AI-generated code.

beats.narration_text: Mine joins the pieces in one small loop that runs on a laptop: sandbox, trace, an independent check, and a human approval before any change leaves. I built it because more and more code is written by agents, and someone has to check it rather than trust it. Along the way I learned Go and Kubernetes, which were both new to me.

sentences.text: Mine joins the pieces in one small loop that runs on a laptop: sandbox, trace, an independent check, and a human approval before any change leaves.
I built it because more and more code is written by agents, and someone has to check it rather than trust it.
Along the way I learned Go and Kubernetes, which were both new to me.

beats.narration_text: Here's one run. The harness starts a Kubernetes pod with no network, not running as root. The agent, Claude Haiku, gets three tools: read a file, write a file, run a command. Every tool call passes a permission policy written in code first. After every change, the harness runs a hidden check the agent never sees. Pass or fail comes only from that check. Then I see the diff and approve it, and my approval is bound to the exact bytes I saw.

The agent, Claude Haiku, gets three tools: read a file, write a file, run a command.
Every tool call passes a permission policy written in code first.
After every change, the harness runs a hidden check the agent never sees.
Pass or fail comes only from that check.

beats.narration_text: The tasks are sixteen small Python repos I made. Eleven are ordinary bugs. Five are designed so the right answer is no: a wrong test, a task that needs the network, a budget too small. I froze a development and held-out split before tuning anything. It runs on my laptop with Docker and kind, a spend-limited API key, and Claude Code, which writes the code while I review every change.

beats.narration_text: It's judged on three things. On normal tasks, it should pass. On the five no-tasks, it must say no. A pass on one of those would mean it failed. Third, I compare changes, like two different system prompts, on held-out tasks nobody tuned on, and I wrote my predictions down before the held-out runs.

beats.narration_text: First results: seventy held-out runs. Both prompts passed all twenty normal runs and said no on all fifteen no-runs. Then I read all forty passing fixes myself. On one task, seven of ten missed what the documentation asks for. So a pass means the checks passed, not that the spec was met.

beats.narration_text: Three things are left. First, a controlled failure: I'll make an agent edit its own test on purpose, show the check catching it, and fix it. Second, a stranger will run the project from the README on a clean machine. Third, I'll harden the check, so it confirms every test actually ran.

beats.narration_text: The biggest risk is a pass that isn't real, since code under test can fool a check. That's why I review diffs and write down every known gap. It won't be a hosted service or a model benchmark. It's one honest tool. Thanks for watching. The code is at github.com/tushar-patel28/agent-proving-ground.
